I'm Jeevan, and my sister Deepika had to give a two-minute talk on turtles in class on Monday.
On Saturday she sat on the bed with her eyes shut, whispering. "I'm pretending I'm in class," she said. "Everyone looking at me."
Then she stood at the cupboard mirror: "Good morning. Did you know turtles lived with the dinosaurs?" Five times, each louder.
The first point went fine. At "how they lay eggs" she stopped. Blank. Again. Blank.
So she wrote "EGGS ON THE BEACH" on a small card and practised until she didn't need to look.
On Monday she came home and said, "I only looked at the card once."

She drew a tiny cloud on the back of her hand. Cloud meant condensation. She practised three more times, glancing at it.
Monday. In front of the class, she looked at her hand once, and kept going.

He lay in bed and went through the day in his head. Seven-thirty bus from the corner. Change at the depot. Walk from the bus stand to the office, maybe ten minutes. Wait in the hall. Hand over the file with his certificates.
He stopped. Ten minutes walking. In this rain. And the file was a cardboard folder.
He sat up. His mother Usha was still awake in the kitchen. "Amma, do we have a plastic cover? Big enough for this file?"
She found one from an old calendar. He slid the folder inside, taped the edge, and put the whole thing in his school bag.
The next morning the rain was so heavy that his shoes squelched. The certificates arrived dry.

"What are you doing?"
"Walking through tomorrow," Kamal said. "Leave at eight. Walk to the station. Local train, twenty-five minutes. Then walk to the college. Find Room 12. Wait. Go in, hand over my documents."
He opened his eyes. "Wait. It's July. What if it's pouring when I walk from the station?"
"You'll get wet."
"I don't care about me. My mark sheets are in a paper envelope." Kamal frowned. "And I don't have an umbrella that closes properly."
Gautam Mama went inside and came back with a zip-lock pouch and his own umbrella. "Here. Both."
Kamal put the envelope in the pouch and felt his shoulders drop. "Now I can sleep."

Zeynep was in charge of the Year 10 cricket match against the school across town in Nairobi. Two weeks before, she looked at the fixture sheet and asked herself, what if it rains?
The long rains had started early. If the match was washed out, both teams would go home and the season would end without it.
So she wrote Plan B underneath. First, she asked the PE office if the indoor hall was free on the same afternoon. It was, from two to five. An indoor six-a-side game with a tennis ball would do. Second, she asked both coaches to hold the following Saturday as a reserve date.
Her teammate Abebe laughed. "You planned a match that hasn't even been rained on yet."
On the day, it poured at one. By two, both teams were in the hall, playing six-a-side. Nobody went home.

"What if it rains?" she said to Sudha Ma'am, the games teacher. "It's July. If it's washed out, the final gets cancelled and the Class 12 girls never get to play before they leave."
Sudha Ma'am raised her eyebrows. "So what's your plan?"
Afreen took out her notebook. "Plan A: ground at nine. Plan B: if it's raining at eight, we move to the indoor hall and play tennis-ball cricket, six a side. Plan C: if the hall's taken, we use next Saturday. Can you book both?"
Ma'am booked the hall and wrote next Saturday in the register.
It drizzled at eight. By nine, both houses were in the hall, cheering.

Trisha was organising the craft fair for women weavers in Mahuva, a small town near the coast, and she had booked the big community hall, which held two hundred. But last year only forty people had come, and the empty hall had felt sad.
This time, three weeks before, she sat in the panchayat office with her friend Bidisha and wrote a rule. "If fewer than sixty weavers and buyers confirm by Friday at six, we move to the smaller school hall." She told the school headmaster the same day, and he agreed to keep it free.
"Why decide now?" Bidisha asked.
"Because on the day I'll be panicking and want to hope for the best," Trisha said.
On Friday at six, the count was fifty-one. Trisha didn't argue with herself. She called the school and the community hall, and sent a message to all fifty-one: new venue, same time.
The school hall was full and lively.

Her friend Dalia said, "Just book the big one. People always come."
"Last year they didn't," Ulla said. "Half the tables were empty." She opened her laptop. "So here's the rule. If fewer than sixty people have signed up by Friday noon, we move to the library room. If it's sixty or more, we keep the hall."

I'm Keerthana, and last year I led the move of our NGO's records to a new online system. I was determined nothing would catch us off guard.
So I wrote backup plans. What if the internet fails. What if the vendor shuts down. What if a volunteer deletes a file. What if there's a flood in the office. What if the software has a virus. Twelve risks, each with a two-page plan. My colleague Charu said, "Most of these won't happen." I said, better safe.
It took me three weeks. I felt very prepared.
What I hadn't done was the actual work. I hadn't cleaned the old data, trained the six volunteers, or tested the import even once.
On migration day, half the records came in with broken dates. Nobody knew how to fix them. None of my twelve plans covered it, because it wasn't a disaster. It was just the main job, not done.

Supervisor's note, project review, 18 October

Her risk file is impressive: fourteen contingency plans, from server failure to a monsoon flooding the data centre to a vendor going bankrupt. Each has a flowchart. Baljeet, the developer on her team, told me she had spent most of September on them.

subtype: Approach: leaves extra time before something starts [Action]
passage:
The school bus stop in Kalyan was a twenty-minute walk, and the monsoon had come. Last Monday, Yusuf left exactly twenty minutes before the bus. His friend Tarun stopped him at the gate to talk about cricket. Yusuf reached the stop just as the doors were closing and had to bang on them.
On Tuesday night he said to his mother, "I'm leaving at thirty minutes before."
"Why ten extra?"
"In case someone stops me. Or the road is flooded. Or I forget something."
On Wednesday, it poured, and the usual lane was knee-deep. He took the long way round. Tarun waved from a shop; Yusuf only waved back.
He reached the stop with four minutes to spare, wet but on time. The bus came. He climbed in, grinning.

qa.q: How many minutes to spare did Yusuf have on Wednesday?
qa.a: He reached the stop with four minutes to spare.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when he climbed onto the bus?
qa.a: He felt pleased and relieved, grinning because the extra ten minutes worked even in the rain.

qa.q: What else could Yusuf do on very rainy days, and why?
qa.a: He could leave a few minutes earlier still, since flooded lanes can use up most of the extra time.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when Yusuf only waves back?
qa.a: Tarun may feel a little left out, but likely understands Yusuf is trying not to miss the bus.

grounding: It shows a boy who takes twenty minutes to reach the bus stop starting to leave thirty minutes before after nearly missing the bus when a friend stopped him.
